The switch jumps to case 2. Without a break the program falls through into case 3, prints 3 and then break ends the switch before case 4.
Arguments are passed by value, so swap works on copies and x and y stay unchanged. The values would only be swapped if pointers were passed.

15 % 2 is 1, so the condition is false and the expression after the colon is used: 3 × 15 + 1 = 46. The value 7 would be x / 2 in integer division.

q: A variable declared inside a function is visible:
o: In every function of the file
x: It is a local variable whose scope is the block in which it is declared. Visibility in all functions needs a global declaration.
i doubles: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. At 16 the condition 16 < 20 is still true, so it doubles once more to 32 and then the loop stops.
The single = assigns 0 to x, and the value of the expression is 0, which counts as false. So the else part runs and prints nonzero.

q: Which return type is used for a function that returns no value?
x: void means no value is returned. null and empty are not C types, and int would require returning an integer.
A do-while executes the body once before testing the condition, so 10 is printed. Afterwards k = 11 and 11 < 10 is false, so the loop ends.

q: When an argument is passed by value, the function:
o: Works on a copy of the argument
Receives the address of the variable
x: A copy is made, so changes inside the function do not alter the caller's variable. Passing the address (a pointer) would allow that.
When i reaches 3, break leaves the loop at once, so 3 is never printed. Only 1 and 2 appear.
The inner call sq(2) is 4, and the outer call sq(4) is 16. The value 8 is 2 × 4, which does not follow from the code.
continue skips the rest of the body for i = 3 only and the loop carries on. So 3 is missing while 4 and 5 are printed.

q: A variable declared outside all functions is called a:
x: A global variable is visible to all functions defined after it. A local variable exists only inside its function.
The inner loop runs 1, 2 and 3 times for i = 1, 2, 3, so c = 1 + 2 + 3 = 6. A full 3 × 3 square would give 9.
The semicolon right after the for makes an empty loop body, so the loop only counts i up to 3. Then printf runs once and prints 3.

q: Which loop always executes its body at least once?
x: The do-while loop tests its condition after the body, so the body runs once even if the condition is false. A for and a while loop test first.

q: Which statement ends the current iteration of a loop and moves on to the next one?
x: continue skips the remaining statements of the current pass and jumps to the next test. break leaves the loop entirely and return leaves the function.

q: Which statement creates an infinite loop?
x: The condition 1 is always true, so the loop never ends. The other loops stop at once or after a single pass.

q: Which of the following is NOT a loop construct?
x: switch selects among cases and does not repeat. The other three repeat a block of statements.
The loop peels off the digits 5, 4, 3 and 2 and adds them: 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 = 14.
The digits are taken from the right: 0, 5, 2, 1, giving r = 0, 5, 52 and 521. A number stored as an int has no leading zero, so 0521 is not printed.
The test n-- uses the old value and then decrements, so inside the body n is already one smaller: 4 down to 0. When the old value is 0 the loop stops.

q: In a `switch` statement, which keyword stops execution from falling through into the next `case`?
x: break ends the switch at once, so the statements of the following cases are skipped. continue belongs to loops, and default only marks the code that runs when no case matches.

q: In a `switch` statement, the statements under the `default` label run when:
o: The first case value matches the expression
No case value matches the switch expression
Every case ends with a break
x: default is the catch-all: control goes there only when none of the case constants equals the value of the expression. A zero expression simply looks for case 0 like any other value.

q: The conditional operator `?:` in C is called a ternary operator because it:
o: Can be nested three levels deep
x: In `cond ? e1 : e2` there are three operands: the condition and two expressions. It still gives only one of two results, so "three possible results" is wrong.

q: In standard C, the expression tested by a `switch` statement must have which type?
x: switch compares the value with integer constants, and a char is stored as a small integer, so int and char work. Floating values and strings cannot be switched on.
72 >= 80 is false and 72 >= 70 is true, so Second is printed and the rest of the chain is skipped. SecondThird would need separate if statements instead of else-if.
These are three separate if statements, not an else-if chain, so each one is tested. 85 passes all three tests, giving PGE; only an else-if chain would stop after P.

An else belongs to the nearest unmatched if, here if (y > 8), whatever the indentation. Since x > 8 is false, the whole inner if-else is skipped and only end is printed; twoend would need braces around the inner if.
Without braces only the first statement belongs to the if. 3 > 5 is false, so big is skipped, but the second printf is outside the if and always runs.
7 % 3 is 1, which matches no case, so control jumps to default and prints X. There is no break after it, so execution falls into case 0, prints Y, and that break ends the switch.
Several case labels can share one group of statements. 'e' matches, the program runs on to printf("vowel"), and break stops it before default.
8 > 12 is false, so the value after the colon, q = 12, is assigned to m. 8 would be chosen only if the condition were true.
n > 0 is false, so the second conditional is evaluated: n < 0 is true, giving -1. The value 0 would be chosen only when n is 0.
a > 5 is false, so the && test fails. In the else-if, b > 5 is true, which makes the || test true, and one is printed.
&& stops as soon as its left side is false (short-circuit). x != 0 is false, so y / x is never computed; the else prints no and then y is printed as 5.
a > 5 is false, so && skips its right side and ++b never runs; b stays 3 and in is not printed. 3 4 would need the right side to be evaluated as well.
In C any non-zero value counts as true, negative numbers included. Only 0 is false, so true is printed.

q: Given `int n = 2;` inside a function, which of these cannot be used as a `case` label in a `switch`?
x: A case label must be a constant expression known at compile time. 'n' is a character constant and 2 + 3 is a constant expression, but n is a variable, so case n: is an error.
1900 % 4 is 0 but 1900 % 100 is also 0, so the bracket is false; 1900 % 400 is 300, not 0, so the whole condition is false. Being divisible by 4 alone is not enough.

q: Which condition is true exactly when `x` is outside the range 1 to 100 (1 and 100 count as inside)?
x: A number is outside when it is below 1 or above 100, so the two tests are joined with ||. No number is both below 1 and above 100, and the <= / >= version and !(x > 1 && x < 100) both wrongly count 1 and 100 as outside.
C evaluates 10 <= x <= 20 from left to right: 10 <= 50 gives 1, then 1 <= 20 gives 1, which is true. So inside is printed even though 50 is outside the range; the right test is x >= 10 && x <= 20.
The semicolon right after if (x > 5) is an empty statement that forms the whole body of the if. The printf("big ") line is therefore not controlled by the if and always runs, followed by end.
No case matches 3 and there is no default, so the switch does nothing. Execution continues after it and prints over.
An else-if chain stops at the first true test: 90 >= 50 is true, so Pass is printed and the m >= 80 branch is never reached. To get Distinction, the m >= 80 test must come first.
m / 10 is integer division, so 87 / 10 gives 8, not 8.7 rounded to 9. Case 8 prints Very good and break ends the switch.
== works from left to right: a == b gives 1, then 1 == c compares 1 with 5, which is 0 (false). So different is printed although all three are equal; the right test is a == b && b == c.
a < b (6 < 2) is false, so the part after the first colon is used: b < c (2 < 9) is true, so m = b = 2, the smallest of the three.
Characters are stored as codes, and the code after 'a' is 'b', so ch holds 'b'. case 'b' prints second and break stops there.
n > 5 is false because 5 is not greater than 5, and ! turns false into true. So small is printed; large would need n to be 6 or more.

q: Which `if-else` does the same job as `y = (x > 0) ? x : -x;`?
x: The value before the colon is used when the condition is true and the one after it when it is false. Writing y = x; y = -x; without else always leaves y equal to -x.

q: In the loop `for (i = 0; i < n; i++)`, which part is executed only once?
x: The initialisation runs once, before the first test. The condition is checked before every pass and i++ runs after every pass.
n takes 10, 7, 4 and 1, and each is printed while n > 0 holds. After 1 it becomes -2, the test fails and -2 is not printed.
i takes 5, 10, 15 and 20, so the body runs 4 times; 25 fails i <= 20. Three would be the count with i < 20.
k takes 1, 3, 5 and 7, so s = 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16; after the last pass k becomes 9, which fails k < 8. 16 7 forgets that k is increased once more before the test.
break leaves only the inner loop. For each i the inner loop prints i with j = 1 and stops at j = 2, and the outer loop carries on: 11 21 31.
continue skips the addition unless i is a multiple of 3, so only 3, 6 and 9 are added: 18. 37 is the sum of the other numbers (55 - 18).
f becomes 1, 2, 6, 24 and 120 as i goes from 1 to 5. 24 would be the result if the loop stopped at i < 5.
A while loop tests first: 5 < 5 is false, so the body never runs and only end is printed. A do-while loop would have printed 5 once.
i takes 10, 5, 2 and 1 (integer division: 5 / 2 is 2 and 1 / 2 is 0), so the body runs 4 times. The loop ends when i becomes 0.
b > a, so b becomes 18 - 12 = 6; then a > b, so a becomes 12 - 6 = 6. Now a equals b, the loop stops and 6 (the HCF of 12 and 18) is printed.
Without continue the count would be 4 × 3 = 12. A pass is skipped when j equals i, which happens for i = 1, 2 and 3 only (j never reaches 4), so c = 12 - 3 = 9.
i becomes 4, 8 and then 12: the test 8 < 10 is still true, so 4 is added once more. At 12 the test fails and 12 is printed.
i takes 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10, and all six satisfy i <= 10. Counting only 2 to 10 gives 5.
n becomes 3, 9, 27 and 81; only 81 is greater than 50, so break leaves the loop there. 27 is the last value that does not exceed 50.
21 % 2 is 1, then 21 % 3 is 0, so break stops the loop with d = 3, the smallest divisor of 21 above 1. 7 also divides 21, but the loop never gets there.
The body prints x and then decreases it, so 3, 2 and 1 are printed. When x becomes 0 the test x > 0 fails, so 0 is not printed.
The inner loop starts at the current i: for i = 1 it prints 123, for i = 2 it prints 23 and for i = 3 just 3, each followed by a space.

q: A function prototype such as `int add(int, int);` tells the compiler:
o: The function's name, return type and parameter types
The statements inside the function body
The values that will be passed in each call
Where the function is stored in memory
x: A prototype declares the function's interface so that calls can be checked before the definition is seen. The body comes only with the definition.

q: The variables named in the header of a function definition, such as `x` and `y` in `int sum(int x, int y)`, are called:
x: Formal parameters receive copies of the values passed. The values written in the call itself, such as sum(3, 4), are the actual arguments.

q: Which is a correct prototype for a function `area` that takes two `int` values and returns a `float`?
x: A prototype gives the return type, then the name, then the parameter types separated by commas, and ends with a semicolon. Swapping int and float describes a different function.

q: Which statement sends a value from a function back to the function that called it?
x: return ends the function and hands its value to the caller. break only leaves a loop or switch, and continue moves to the next pass of a loop.
a receives 3 and b receives 4, so the function returns 3 × 2 + 4 = 10. 11 would come from swapping the arguments (4 × 2 + 3).
Arguments are matched by position, not by name: the parameter x receives 10 and y receives 3, so the result is 10 - 3 = 7. -7 assumes the names are matched.
Inside show the local n (9) hides the global n, so 9 is printed. main has no local n, so it prints the global 5, which show never changed.
g is global, so both calls change the same variable: 1 + 2 = 3, then 3 + 3 = 6. 1 would be right only if add changed a local copy.
The parameter n is a copy, so doubling it inside twice leaves main's n at 4. The returned value 8 is stored in m.
(7 + 8) / 2 is 15 / 2, and dividing two int values drops the fraction, giving 7. An int function cannot return 7.5.
n / 2 divides two ints, so 7 / 2 is 3 before the value is converted to float for the return. %.1f then prints 3.0; 3.5 would need n / 2.0.
For -6 the second test is true and return -1 ends the function. For 0 both tests fail, so the last line returns 0.
return ends the function immediately, so the printf after it never runs. The call gives 4 + 1 = 5.
odd returns 1 for an odd k and 0 for an even k, so only 1, 3 and 5 are added: s = 9. 12 is the sum of the even numbers 2 + 4 + 6.
Without braces the for controls only the first tick(), which runs 4 times; the second tick() runs once after the loop. The global count ends at 5.
c is a local variable, created and set to 0 again on every call, so each call prints 1. 1 2 3 would need c to keep its value between calls, as a global variable does.
The inner calls are done first: add(1, 2) = 3 and add(3, 4) = 7. Then mul(3, 7) = 21; 10 is just the sum 1 + 2 + 3 + 4.

q: A program calls `total()` inside `main()` but defines `total()` after `main()`. What should be written before `main()` so the compiler can check the call?
x: A prototype declares the return type and parameters early, so the compiler can check the call before it reaches the definition. There is no standard header total.h, and a variable with the same name would clash with the function.

q: How many values can a C function send back directly through a single `return` statement?
o: As many as it has parameters
x: `return expression;` gives back exactly one value. The number of parameters has nothing to do with it, and a function that returns nothing is declared void.

q: An ordinary local variable declared inside a function is created and destroyed:
o: When the program starts and when it ends
When the file is compiled and when it is linked
When the function is called and when it returns
Only once, the first time the function runs
x: A local (automatic) variable exists only while its function is running and is created afresh on each call. Lasting from the start to the end of the program is true of global variables.
For 507 the body runs for 507, 50 and 5, giving 3. For 0 the do-while body still runs once before the test, so digits(0) returns 1, not 0.
The parameter x hides the global x inside f, so only the copy becomes 15 and is returned. The global x is untouched, so main then prints 10.
50 >= 50 is true, so the first call returns 'P'; 49 >= 50 is false, so the second returns 'F'. FF comes from reading the test as m > 50.
Inside step the global g becomes 2 × 3 = 6, and the function returns 6 + 3 = 9. The change to g is kept because g is global, so main prints 9 6.

q: Which header file must be included to use `FILE`, `fopen()` and `fclose()`?
x: The file functions belong to the standard input/output library, declared in stdio.h. conio.h is a console header for functions such as getch.

q: Which mode string in `fopen()` opens an existing text file for reading only?
x: "r" opens a file for reading and fails if the file does not exist. "w" and "a" open for writing, and "rw" is not a valid C mode.

q: What does `fgetc(fp)` return when it reaches the end of the file?
x: fgetc returns the constant EOF (usually -1) when no more characters can be read. NULL is what fopen returns when a file cannot be opened.

q: Which statement correctly declares a pointer for working with a file?
x: FILE is a type defined in stdio.h, written in capitals, and the * placed before the name makes fp a pointer to it. The * cannot follow the name or come before the type, and & is not used in a declaration.

q: `marks.txt` already holds 20 lines. What happens when it is opened with `fopen("marks.txt", "w")`?
o: New data is added after the 20 existing lines
fopen fails and returns NULL because the file exists
Its old contents are erased and writing starts in an empty file
The file is opened for reading only
x: Mode "w" creates a new file or cuts an existing one to zero length, so the 20 lines are lost. Adding after the old lines is what mode "a" does.
After the first two openings the file holds ABCD, because "a" adds CD at the end. The last opening with "w" erases everything and writes EF; ABCDEF would need that mode to be "a".

q: A program calls `fopen("notes.txt", "a")`, but `notes.txt` does not exist yet. What happens?
o: A new empty file is created and opened for appending
fopen returns NULL because the file is missing
The program reads from the start of the file
The file is created but opened for reading only
x: Mode "a" creates the file if it is missing, and every write then goes to its end. Returning NULL for a missing file is how mode "r" behaves.

q: What does `fopen("data.txt", "r")` return if `data.txt` does not exist?
o: A pointer to a newly created empty file
A pointer to the end of the file
x: Opening for reading never creates a file; when the file cannot be opened, fopen returns NULL, which a program should test before using fp. EOF is returned by reading functions such as fgetc, not by fopen.
Each fgetc call reads one character and the loop counts it, so the 8 letters give n = 8. When fgetc returns EOF the loop stops without counting it, so 9 is wrong.

q: In `while ((ch = fgetc(fp)) != EOF)`, why is `ch` usually declared as `int` rather than `char`?
o: Because fgetc can read only digits
So it can hold EOF, which differs from every character value
Because a char variable cannot be compared with !=
So that the loop runs faster
x: fgetc returns an int: either a character code or the special value EOF. A plain char may not keep EOF apart from a real character, so the end of the file could be missed or found too early; int avoids this.
fscanf works like scanf but reads from the file, so a = 4, b = 7 and c = 10, and their sum 21 is printed. 4710 would be the numbers written side by side, not added.
fscanf reads 3, 5 and 8, one per pass, so n = 3 and s = 16. The fourth call finds the end of the file and returns EOF, so the loop stops and 8 is not added twice.
fputc writes one character per pass, with nothing between them, for c from 'a' to 'e' inclusive. Mode "w" erases the file only when it is opened, not between writes, so all five letters stay.
fprintf writes to the file the same way printf writes to the screen: 1, 4 and 9, each followed by a comma, including the last one.
Every fgetc call moves on by one character. The first call reads H (not printed), the second reads E and the third reads L, so EL is printed.

q: Which statement opens `marks.txt` so that new records are added at the end without losing the old ones?
x: fopen takes the file name first and the mode second, and mode "a" appends at the end. "w" would erase the old records and "r" does not allow writing.
